newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan to work out China investment indicator.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan to work out China investment indicator.

text.p: Taiwan is considering establishing an indicator system to regulate the flow of investment to rival China, a leading newspaper reported on Monday.

The indicator, which would reflect political and economic conditions on the mainland, could be used by the government to signal when such investment would have the best benefit for Taiwan, the China Times daily said.
Economics officials acknowledged that they would hold a meeting this week to review Taiwan's indirect investment in China, but declined to say whether such a plan was in the works.
"A special task force will convene a meeting later this week to discuss unauthorised investments on the mainland," an economic ministry spokesman told Reuter by telephone.

The official said the review meeting was being held "in view of the increase in unauthorised investments in mainland China and the communists' repeated bids to sabotage our relations with other countries."
The paper said the economic ministry had invited six scholars to work out the China investment indicator system in the face of Beijing's increased attempts to squeeze Taiwan internationally.
Under the draft plan, the indicator would reflect the condition in which Taiwan government should tighten or relax local investments on the mainland, said the daily.
In other words, if relations between the rival sides of the Taiwan Strait turn worse, Taiwan would tighten the indirect investment; otherwise it would loosen its restriction, the paper said.
Taiwan has banned direct investment in China since a civil war split the two in 1949.
But some 30,000 Taiwan firms have poured an estimated US$30 billion through their overseas affiliates in funding their investment on the mainland, a number without government authorisation.

Chang King-yuh, head of Taiwan's top mainland policy planning body the Mainland Affairs Council, on Monday said before parliament that the government would not encourage large investment in China because of Beijing's hostility.
"It is true mainland investment can help promote cross-strait exchange, but if there is no restraint, those investments might end up into being held hostaged," Chang said.
He said before China stops its military threats against Taiwan and efforts to sabotage Taipei's international relations, it would be risky for local firms to invest on the mainland.
China, which has viewed Taiwan as a rebel-held province with no rights to participate in international affairs, has pressured Taiwan's Latin American diplomatic allies into breaking ties with Taipei.
Taiwan is left with 30 diplomatic allies, 16 from Latin America, following its 48 years of diplomatic war with China.

The Nationalist island has decided to put a cap on local investments in China after footwear giant Pou Chen reportedly invest in setting up a bank in China, and petrochemcial giant Formosa Plastic 1301TW group reportedly starting a thermal power plant project on the mainland.

Although Taiwan allows its businessmen to invest indirectly to the mainland since late 1980s, it still bars them from investing in key industries like power and auto plants, as well as financial services.
Still a number of firms have used their overseas affiliates to skirt the ban for unauthorised investments in China.
